groups.title: Demography
groups.description: The size and shape of the birth cohort the model follows from birth to five years.

groups.title: Epidemiology
groups.description: How often RSV occurs in the first year of life, how severe it is and how it is distributed over the calendar year.

groups.title: Health system costs
groups.description: What one case of each type costs the health system, in the currency and the price year of the analysis.

groups.title: QALY losses
groups.description: The health-related quality of life lost per case, used to convert cases into QALYs.

groups.title: Maternal RSV vaccine
groups.description: Efficacy, protection duration, coverage, price and delivery costs of the maternal vaccine.

groups.title: Monoclonal antibody
groups.description: Efficacy, protection duration, coverage, price and delivery costs of the monoclonal antibody.

groups.title: Analysis conventions
groups.description: Perspective, discounting and the willingness-to-pay thresholds used for the decision analysis.

questions.label: Annual births
questions.definition: The number of live births in the country in the price year of the analysis. The model follows a single birth cohort of this size from birth to 60 months of age.
questions.why_it_matters: Every burden estimate scales with it: cases, admissions, deaths, costs and QALYs are all proportional to the cohort size.
questions.how_to_source: National statistics office (birth registrations) or the UN World Population Prospects; a World Bank crude birth rate applied to the population of the same year also works, but say so in the source.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads the cohort size from a country-details file.

questions.evidence_guidance: Direct national count. Use `ok` with the statistics-office citation; `transfer` if a regional estimate stands in.

questions.label: Stillbirth rate
questions.definition: The share of pregnancies that end in a stillbirth. The cohort that enters the model is births × (1 − stillbirth rate).
questions.why_it_matters: A stillbirth rate that is too low inflates every burden estimate. It also changes the number of doses the maternal programme has to deliver, because the vaccine is given during pregnancy.
questions.how_to_source: National perinatal registry or vital statistics; WHO and UNICEF country estimates are an acceptable transfer.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation takes it from the same country-details file as the births.

questions.evidence_guidance: National registry: `ok`. Regional estimate: `transfer`.

questions.label: Pre-term birth rate
questions.definition: The share of live births before 37 weeks of gestation. The maternal vaccine is given to the mother, so a pre-term infant is effectively unprotected: maternal coverage is scaled by (1 − pre-term rate).
questions.why_it_matters: Too low a value overstates the benefit of the maternal vaccine; too high a value understates it.
questions.how_to_source: National perinatal registry; WHO/UNICEF estimates; the McMarcel configuration reads it as the incomplete maternal transfer rate.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads the pre-term rate from the country-details file.

questions.evidence_guidance: National registry: `ok`. Regional estimate: `transfer`.

questions.label: Life expectancy at birth
questions.definition: Life expectancy at birth, used only when the pack does not carry a life table asset and the engine has to generate one.
questions.why_it_matters: It drives the years of life lost by an RSV death and therefore the QALY loss of deaths.
questions.how_to_source: National life table, or the UN World Population Prospects for the same year and country.
questions.evidence_guidance: Official life table: `ok`. UN estimate: `transfer`.

questions.label: Mean population utility
questions.definition: The average health-related quality of life of the general population. It is used to turn life expectancy into health-related QALYs when the life table has to be generated.
questions.why_it_matters: Deaths are converted into QALYs with the life table, so this value scales the mortality-related part of the QALY loss.
questions.how_to_source: A national or regional EQ-5D / EQ-VAS population norm set (the reference implementation uses the Belgian 2018 EQ-5D norms).

reference_sources.note: EQ-5D Belgian general population norms (BE, 2018) used by the reference implementation.

questions.evidence_guidance: Population norms: `ok` with the survey citation. Norms from another country: `transfer`.

questions.label: Hospital incidence, 0–5 months
questions.definition: The number of hospital admissions for RSV per infant in the first five months of life. The engine scales it to the cohort and distributes it over the calendar months with the seasonality profile.
questions.why_it_matters: It is the single largest driver of the burden: every downstream outcome (deaths, costs, QALYs) is proportional to it.
questions.how_to_source: National hospital discharge data (ICD-10 J21 or the local RSV code) per age in months, for at least two seasons so that a seasonal profile can be derived.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads a 60 × 12 age-by-calendar-month admission matrix and scales it to the cohort.

questions.evidence_guidance: National discharge data: `ok` with the extraction described. Adjusted or modelled rates: `derived` with the derivation recorded.

questions.label: Hospital incidence, 6–11 months
questions.definition: The number of hospital admissions for RSV per infant between six and eleven months of age.
questions.why_it_matters: The second RSV season is much smaller than the first, so this value determines how much of the burden sits outside the first year — where catch-up programmes and the protection duration matter most.
questions.how_to_source: Same source as the 0–5 month incidence, split by age in months.
questions.evidence_guidance: National discharge data: `ok`. Modelled: `derived`.

questions.label: Outpatient to hospital ratio
questions.definition: The number of outpatient consultations per hospital admission. The engine converts the hospital admission profile into outpatient cases and spreads them over the calendar months with the hospital seasonality.
questions.why_it_matters: Outpatient cases dominate the number of cases and carry a unit cost and a QALY loss each, so the ratio drives most of the total cost.
questions.how_to_source: Ambulatory (outpatient) data for the same population and period, divided by the admission count of the same period.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation uses outpatient incidence per 1,000 infant-months, with epidemiological samples for the uncertainty.

questions.evidence_guidance: National ambulatory data: `ok`. Ratio borrowed from another country: `transfer`.

questions.label: Non-medically-attended proportion
questions.definition: The share of medically attended RSV cases that never reach a clinician (pharmacy advice, telephone advice, no care). The engine adds these cases on top of the attended ones.
questions.why_it_matters: They add cases and costs but are invisible in hospital and outpatient data, so they are often underestimated.
questions.how_to_source: Household surveys, retail pharmacy sales data or sentinel primary-care data for the same period.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads a sample of non-medically-attended proportions by age month.

questions.evidence_guidance: National survey: `ok`. Regional pharmacy data: `transfer`.

questions.label: ICU share of hospital admissions
questions.definition: The number of ICU admissions per hospital admission. Only used when the pack does not carry an ICU matrix.
questions.why_it_matters: ICU cases carry the highest unit cost and the highest case-fatality risk, so this value moves the cost and the death estimates.
questions.how_to_source: National ICU registry or hospital discharge data with an intensive-care flag.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads a separate 60 × 12 ICU matrix.

questions.evidence_guidance: National registry: `ok`. Literature estimate: `transfer`.

questions.label: Hospital case-fatality risk
questions.definition: The probability that a child hospitalised with RSV dies, by age in months. The engine multiplies the admissions with this risk to obtain deaths.
questions.why_it_matters: Deaths drive the life-years and health-related QALYs lost, so this value has an outsized effect on the QALY loss and on every cost-effectiveness ratio.
questions.how_to_source: National hospital mortality data by age (discharge diagnosis RSV), or the published case-fatality series used by the framework.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads the age-specific hospital and ICU case-fatality risks from one file.

questions.evidence_guidance: National mortality data: `ok`. Published series from another country: `transfer`.

questions.label: ICU case-fatality risk
questions.definition: The probability that a child admitted to intensive care with RSV dies, by age in months.
questions.why_it_matters: ICU deaths are the most expensive and the most damaging in QALY terms, so this value can dominate the mortality estimate.
questions.how_to_source: National ICU registry or hospital mortality data by age.

reference_sources.note: Same file as the hospital case-fatality risk.

questions.evidence_guidance: National registry: `ok`. Published series: `transfer`.

questions.label: Hospital age decay
questions.definition: The monthly factor by which the hospital admission rate falls with age. A factor of 1 means the rate does not decay; 0.97 means three per cent less each month.
questions.why_it_matters: The engine uses it to build an age profile when no admission matrix is supplied, so it shapes the whole burden curve.
questions.how_to_source: Fit the decay to the national age profile of RSV admissions, or set it to 1 when a full age-by-month matrix is supplied.
questions.evidence_guidance: Fitted to national data: `derived`, with the fit described. A default: `convention`.

questions.label: Outpatient age decay
questions.definition: The monthly factor by which the outpatient rate falls with age, used when no outpatient matrix is supplied.
questions.why_it_matters: Together with the hospital profile it sets the shape of the outpatient burden, which is the largest cost component.
questions.how_to_source: Fit to the national age profile of outpatient consultations, or set it to 1 when a matrix is supplied.
questions.evidence_guidance: Fitted to national data: `derived`. A default: `convention`.

questions.label: Case-fatality age decay
questions.definition: The monthly factor by which the case-fatality risk falls with age, used when no case-fatality profile is supplied.
questions.why_it_matters: It changes how the deaths are distributed over the first year of life.
questions.how_to_source: Fit to the national age profile of RSV deaths, or set it to 1 when an age profile is supplied.
questions.evidence_guidance: Fitted to national data: `derived`. A default: `convention`.

questions.label: Seasonality amplitude
questions.definition: The strength of the calendar-month seasonality of RSV admissions. Zero is a flat year, 0.8 is a very peaked year with a December maximum.
questions.why_it_matters: Seasonality decides which birth cohorts are inside a seasonal programme window, and therefore how much a catch-up programme can add.
questions.how_to_source: Derive it from the national age-by-calendar-month admission matrix (or set it to 0 and supply the matrix itself).
questions.evidence_guidance: Derived from national data: `derived`. A default: `convention`.

questions.label: Outpatient cost per case
questions.definition: The cost of one outpatient RSV consultation, in the currency of the analysis and in the price year.
questions.why_it_matters: Outpatient cases are the most frequent, so this value contributes a large part of the medical cost that prevention can avert.
questions.how_to_source: Insurance claims, national tariff or costing study for the price year; convert with the price-year index and state the index used.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads the unit costs per perspective and region, with a mean and a confidence interval or standard deviation.

questions.evidence_guidance: National tariff or claims for the price year: `ok` with the citation. Cost from another country: `transfer`. An international reference price: `transfer` with the country named.

questions.label: Outpatient cost per case, standard deviation
questions.definition: The standard deviation of the sampled unit cost. The engine samples the cost from a gamma distribution with this mean and standard deviation.
questions.why_it_matters: A cost without uncertainty understates the width of the cost-effectiveness plane and can hide a strategy that is not robust.
questions.how_to_source: Derive it from the published confidence interval of the cost as (upper − lower) / (2 × 1.96), or from the variability of the claims.
questions.evidence_guidance: Derived from a published interval: `derived`, with the interval cited. A zero standard deviation is a convention: say so.

questions.label: Hospital cost per admission
questions.definition: The cost of one hospital admission for RSV, excluding intensive care, in the currency of the analysis and the price year.
questions.why_it_matters: Hospital cost is the largest cost per case and the value that the cost-effectiveness result is most sensitive to.
questions.how_to_source: Insurance claims or a national tariff; state whether the cost includes the admission and the ward stay only.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads the unit costs per perspective and region, with a mean and a confidence interval or standard deviation.

questions.evidence_guidance: National tariff or claims for the price year: `ok` with the citation. Cost from another country: `transfer`. An international reference price: `transfer` with the country named.

questions.definition: The standard deviation of the sampled unit cost. The engine samples the cost from a gamma distribution with this mean and standard deviation.
questions.why_it_matters: A cost without uncertainty understates the width of the cost-effectiveness plane and can hide a strategy that is not robust.
questions.how_to_source: Derive it from the published confidence interval of the cost as (upper − lower) / (2 × 1.96), or from the variability of the claims.
questions.evidence_guidance: Derived from a published interval: `derived`, with the interval cited. A zero standard deviation is a convention: say so.

questions.definition: The cost of one intensive-care admission for RSV, in the currency of the analysis and the price year.
questions.why_it_matters: ICU cases are few but expensive; they dominate the tail of the cost distribution.
questions.how_to_source: Insurance claims or a national tariff for intensive care.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads the unit costs per perspective and region, with a mean and a confidence interval or standard deviation.

questions.evidence_guidance: National tariff or claims for the price year: `ok` with the citation. Cost from another country: `transfer`. An international reference price: `transfer` with the country named.

questions.label: Non-medically-attended cost per case
questions.definition: The cost of managing one case that never reaches a clinician, in the currency of the analysis and the price year.
questions.why_it_matters: Small per case, but these cases are frequent, so the total is not negligible.
questions.how_to_source: Pharmacy costs, telephone consultation tariffs or a costing study of the non-attended pathway.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation reads the unit costs per perspective and region, with a mean and a confidence interval or standard deviation.

questions.evidence_guidance: National tariff or claims for the price year: `ok` with the citation. Cost from another country: `transfer`. An international reference price: `transfer` with the country named.

questions.label: Wheezing sequelae cost
questions.definition: The cost per child-year of recurrent wheezing and asthma after an RSV hospital admission.
questions.why_it_matters: The recurrent-wheezing module is not implemented in this engine version, so this value is not applied to the results.
questions.how_to_source: If you have a value, keep it and document that the engine cannot apply it yet; otherwise set it to zero and record the omission.

questions.label: QALY loss, outpatient
questions.definition: The health-related quality of life lost by one outpatient RSV case, in QALYs per case.
questions.why_it_matters: Outpatient cases are the most frequent, so this value determines most of the non-fatal QALY loss.
questions.how_to_source: Published utility decrements for acute respiratory infection in children, adapted to the local setting, or an EQ-5D study of RSV cases.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation hard-codes the Belgian QALY losses and derives their standard error from the published confidence interval.

questions.evidence_guidance: Published decrements for the same country: `ok` with the citation. Decrement from another country: `transfer`, with the adaptation described.

questions.label: QALY loss, outpatient, standard deviation
questions.definition: The standard deviation of the sampled utility loss, derived from the published confidence interval.
questions.why_it_matters: It controls how wide the QALY uncertainty is and therefore how often a strategy changes rank.
questions.how_to_source: Derive it from the published confidence interval as (upper − lower) / (2 × 1.96).
questions.evidence_guidance: Derived from a published interval: `derived`, with the interval cited.

questions.label: QALY loss, hospital
questions.definition: The health-related quality of life lost by one hospitalised RSV case, in QALYs per case. The same value is applied to ICU cases.
questions.why_it_matters: It converts the most severe and most expensive cases into QALYs.
questions.how_to_source: Published utility decrements for hospitalised RSV in infants, or a local EQ-5D follow-up of hospitalised cases.

reference_sources.note: The reference implementation hard-codes the Belgian QALY losses and derives their standard error from the published confidence interval.

questions.evidence_guidance: Published decrements for the same country: `ok` with the citation. Decrement from another country: `transfer`, with the adaptation described.

questions.how_to_source: Derive it from the published confidence interval as (upper − lower) / (2 × 1.96).
questions.evidence_guidance: Derived from a published interval: `derived`, with the interval cited.

questions.label: QALY loss, non-medically-attended

questions.why_it_matters: These cases are frequent, so a plausible but wrong value can dominate the QALY loss.
questions.how_to_source: Published decrements for ambulatory respiratory infection, or a survey of families of children with RSV.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine efficacy, hospitalisation
questions.definition: The efficacy of the product against RSV hospitalisation.
questions.why_it_matters: Hospital admissions are the most expensive outcome, so this value drives the cost-effectiveness of the programme.
questions.how_to_source: The pivotal trial or its pooled estimate for the same age group and outcome, with its confidence interval.

reference_sources.note: Efficacy against medically attended infection, by age, with bootstrap samples.
Efficacy against hospitalisation, by age, with bootstrap samples.
Efficacy against the severe composite, by age, with bootstrap samples.

questions.evidence_guidance: Trial estimate for the same country or a multi-country trial including it: `ok` with the citation. Estimate from another setting: `transfer`, with the population named.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine efficacy, hospitalisation: standard deviation
questions.definition: The standard deviation of the sampled efficacy, derived from the confidence interval of the trial estimate.
questions.why_it_matters: It decides how often the programme misses its expected effect, and therefore how often the cost-effectiveness result changes.
questions.how_to_source: Derive it from the published confidence interval as (upper − lower) / (2 × 1.96), or from the bootstrap distribution in the efficacy file.
questions.evidence_guidance: Derived from a published interval: `derived`, with the interval cited.

questions.why_it_matters: Most cases are outpatient, so this value determines the number of cases the programme averts.
questions.how_to_source: The pivotal trial estimate for the same outcome and age group, with its confidence interval.

questions.how_to_source: The trial estimate for the severe composite, or the intensive-care efficacy with the reasoning recorded.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine protection duration
questions.definition: How long the protection lasts after the dose is given. The engine applies the efficacy for that many months of age.
questions.why_it_matters: A duration that is too long credits the programme with protection it does not give, and a duration that is too short understates it.
questions.how_to_source: The trial follow-up that supports the duration, or the regulatory label. State whether the protection wanes over time; if it does, supply an age-specific efficacy profile instead.
questions.evidence_guidance: Trial follow-up: `ok` with the citation. Regulatory label: `ok`.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine coverage
questions.definition: The share of the eligible cohort that receives the product. Every scenario can override it; this value is the default.
questions.why_it_matters: Coverage scales the whole benefit linearly, so it is the assumption an analyst is most often asked to defend.
questions.how_to_source: The coverage assumed in the study protocol, the expected uptake in the first year, or the national immunisation coverage for a comparable programme.
questions.evidence_guidance: Planned programme coverage from the study protocol: `ok`. Observed coverage from another country: `transfer`.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine price, low
questions.definition: The lower bound of the dose price. When the two price bounds are equal, the price is deterministic.
questions.why_it_matters: The price drives the intervention cost, which is the dominant term in the incremental cost, and it drives the price threshold P*.
questions.how_to_source: The confidential price from the manufacturer, the price used in the study protocol, or a published reference price. Always record the price year and whether the price is confidential.
questions.evidence_guidance: Study price: `ok` with the citation. List price: `ok`. Reference price from another country: `transfer`.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine price, high
questions.definition: The upper bound of the dose price, sampled uniformly between the low and the high bound.
questions.why_it_matters: A price range widens the cost-effectiveness plane and shows how much the conclusion depends on the price.
questions.how_to_source: The same source as the low bound; a scenario analysis range is a legitimate choice if it is documented as such.
questions.evidence_guidance: Same status as the low bound.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine administration cost
questions.definition: The cost of delivering one dose: the health-care professional time and the consumables, per dose.
questions.why_it_matters: It is added to the price of every dose, so it matters most for expensive products with small cohorts.
questions.how_to_source: The programme budget or the costing study of the delivery pathway.
questions.evidence_guidance: Programme budget: `ok`. Unit-costing study: `ok`.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine implementation cost
questions.definition: The fixed cost of setting the programme up (training, information, cold chain), divided over the doses of the cohort.
questions.why_it_matters: It is a fixed cost spread over one cohort, so it matters most for small cohorts and for expensive products.
questions.how_to_source: The programme budget for the first year.
questions.evidence_guidance: Programme budget: `ok`.

questions.label: Maternal RSV vaccine wastage
questions.definition: The share of doses that are lost: multi-dose vials, missed appointments, wastage at the end of the campaign.
questions.why_it_matters: Wastage raises the number of doses that have to be bought, and therefore the intervention cost.
questions.how_to_source: The programme's own wastage rate, or the wastage rate of a comparable immunisation programme in the same health system.
questions.evidence_guidance: Programme data: `ok`. Comparable programme: `transfer`.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody efficacy, hospitalisation
questions.definition: The efficacy of the product against RSV hospitalisation.
questions.why_it_matters: Hospital admissions are the most expensive outcome, so this value drives the cost-effectiveness of the programme.
questions.how_to_source: The pivotal trial or its pooled estimate for the same age group and outcome, with its confidence interval.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody efficacy, hospitalisation: standard deviation
questions.definition: The standard deviation of the sampled efficacy, derived from the confidence interval of the trial estimate.
questions.why_it_matters: It decides how often the programme misses its expected effect, and therefore how often the cost-effectiveness result changes.
questions.how_to_source: Derive it from the published confidence interval as (upper − lower) / (2 × 1.96), or from the bootstrap distribution in the efficacy file.
questions.evidence_guidance: Derived from a published interval: `derived`, with the interval cited.

questions.definition: The efficacy of the product against RSV death. The reference implementation sets this equal to the intensive-care efficacy.
questions.why_it_matters: Deaths are the outcome with the largest quality-of-life consequence, so this value matters even though it is not observed directly in most trials.
questions.how_to_source: The trial estimate for the severe composite, or the intensive-care efficacy with the reasoning recorded.

questions.definition: The efficacy of the product against RSV infection that never reaches a clinician.
questions.why_it_matters: These cases are frequent; an efficacy of zero here means the programme only prevents visible disease.
questions.how_to_source: The trial estimate for the same outcome, or the all-cause efficacy with the reasoning recorded.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody protection duration
questions.definition: How long the protection lasts after the dose is given. The engine applies the efficacy for that many months of age.
questions.why_it_matters: A duration that is too long credits the programme with protection it does not give, and a duration that is too short understates it.
questions.how_to_source: The trial follow-up that supports the duration, or the regulatory label. State whether the protection wanes over time; if it does, supply an age-specific efficacy profile instead.
questions.evidence_guidance: Trial follow-up: `ok` with the citation. Regulatory label: `ok`.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody coverage
questions.definition: The share of the eligible cohort that receives the product. Every scenario can override it; this value is the default.
questions.why_it_matters: Coverage scales the whole benefit linearly, so it is the assumption an analyst is most often asked to defend.
questions.how_to_source: The coverage assumed in the study protocol, the expected uptake in the first year, or the national immunisation coverage for a comparable programme.
questions.evidence_guidance: Planned programme coverage from the study protocol: `ok`. Observed coverage from another country: `transfer`.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody price, low
questions.definition: The lower bound of the dose price. When the two price bounds are equal, the price is deterministic.
questions.why_it_matters: The price drives the intervention cost, which is the dominant term in the incremental cost, and it drives the price threshold P*.
questions.how_to_source: The confidential price from the manufacturer, the price used in the study protocol, or a published reference price. Always record the price year and whether the price is confidential.
questions.evidence_guidance: Study price: `ok` with the citation. List price: `ok`. Reference price from another country: `transfer`.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody price, high
questions.definition: The upper bound of the dose price, sampled uniformly between the low and the high bound.
questions.why_it_matters: A price range widens the cost-effectiveness plane and shows how much the conclusion depends on the price.
questions.how_to_source: The same source as the low bound; a scenario analysis range is a legitimate choice if it is documented as such.
questions.evidence_guidance: Same status as the low bound.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody administration cost
questions.definition: The cost of delivering one dose: the health-care professional time and the consumables, per dose.
questions.why_it_matters: It is added to the price of every dose, so it matters most for expensive products with small cohorts.
questions.how_to_source: The programme budget or the costing study of the delivery pathway.
questions.evidence_guidance: Programme budget: `ok`. Unit-costing study: `ok`.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody implementation cost
questions.definition: The fixed cost of setting the programme up (training, information, cold chain), divided over the doses of the cohort.
questions.why_it_matters: It is a fixed cost spread over one cohort, so it matters most for small cohorts and for expensive products.
questions.how_to_source: The programme budget for the first year.
questions.evidence_guidance: Programme budget: `ok`.

questions.label: Monoclonal antibody wastage
questions.definition: The share of doses that are lost: multi-dose vials, missed appointments, wastage at the end of the campaign.
questions.why_it_matters: Wastage raises the number of doses that have to be bought, and therefore the intervention cost.
questions.how_to_source: The programme's own wastage rate, or the wastage rate of a comparable immunisation programme in the same health system.
questions.evidence_guidance: Programme data: `ok`. Comparable programme: `transfer`.

questions.label: Cost discount rate
questions.definition: The annual rate at which future costs are discounted.
questions.why_it_matters: Discounting lowers the value of a prevention programme whose costs are now and whose benefits are later, or the other way round when the intervention is cheap and durable.
questions.how_to_source: The national guideline on health-economic evaluation; the reference implementation uses 3 %.
questions.evidence_guidance: National guideline: `ok` with the citation. A convention: `convention`.

questions.label: Effect discount rate
questions.definition: The annual rate at which future health effects are discounted.
questions.why_it_matters: It changes the weight of the deaths averted in the first months of life against the cases averted later.
questions.how_to_source: The national guideline; the reference implementation uses 1.5 %.
questions.evidence_guidance: National guideline: `ok` with the citation. A convention: `convention`.

questions.label: GDP per capita
questions.definition: The gross domestic product per capita of the country in the price year. It is only used to derive the willingness-to-pay thresholds.
questions.why_it_matters: The thresholds decide at which price a strategy is considered good value for money, so the GDP choice shapes the headline conclusion.
questions.how_to_source: National accounts (Eurostat, World Bank) for the price year, in the currency of the analysis.
questions.evidence_guidance: National accounts: `ok` with the citation. International estimate: `transfer`.

questions.label: Exchange rate, local currency per USD
questions.definition: The exchange rate used to convert a dollar value into the currency of the analysis.
questions.why_it_matters: Only needed when a source is reported in dollars; the engine itself works in the local currency.
questions.how_to_source: The central bank or the international source that published the dollar figure.
questions.evidence_guidance: Central bank: `ok`.

questions.label: Willingness-to-pay threshold, 0.5 × GDP per capita
questions.definition: The lower decision threshold: half of GDP per capita per QALY.
questions.why_it_matters: It is a decision convention, not an estimate; the results are reported against all three thresholds so that the reader can judge the choice.
questions.how_to_source: The study protocol or the national guideline that sets the threshold.
questions.evidence_guidance: Decision convention: `convention`, with the protocol cited.

questions.label: Willingness-to-pay threshold, 1 × GDP per capita
questions.definition: The central decision threshold: one times GDP per capita per QALY.
questions.why_it_matters: It is the threshold most often used for the headline conclusion.
questions.how_to_source: The study protocol or the national guideline that sets the threshold.
questions.evidence_guidance: Decision convention: `convention`, with the protocol cited.

questions.label: Willingness-to-pay threshold, 3 × GDP per capita
questions.definition: The upper decision threshold: three times GDP per capita per QALY.
questions.why_it_matters: It shows which strategies become good value for money under a more generous threshold.
questions.how_to_source: The study protocol or the national guideline that sets the threshold.
questions.evidence_guidance: Decision convention: `convention`, with the protocol cited.

questions.label: Analysis perspective
questions.definition: Whose costs and benefits are counted: the health-care payer, the health system, or society.
questions.why_it_matters: A societal perspective adds productivity losses, which the current engine does not model; say which perspective the results are in.
questions.how_to_source: The study protocol and the national guideline.
questions.evidence_guidance: Decision convention: `convention`, with the protocol cited.

questions.label: Currency
questions.definition: The ISO 4217 code of the currency in which every monetary value of the pack is expressed.
questions.why_it_matters: All costs have to be in the same currency; the engine does not convert them.
questions.how_to_source: The study protocol and the price year.
questions.evidence_guidance: Fact: `ok`.
